title: Amos 6:1–14
context: Amos pronounces woe on the leaders who are “at ease in Zion” and “secure on the mountain of Samaria,” lounging on ivory beds while they are “not grieved for the affliction of Joseph.” The Lord GOD then swears by himself that he abhors the pride of Jacob. The chapter closes with the LORD raising up a nation to afflict Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of the Arabah, the same northern limit that 2 Kings 14:25 gives for Jeroboam’s restored border. Shared ground: comfort that ignores others’ ruin is a sin God judges.

verses.text: Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who are secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel come!
verses.arminianNotes: Amos’s woe falls on “those who are at ease in Zion” and secure in Samaria. Arminian readers note that Judah is included alongside Israel: complacency is a danger for every people who assume God’s favor without living faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same warning to all who rest in privilege, and note that the leaders were the ones the house of Israel came to for help. Shared ground: those with influence carry greater responsibility, and ease built on pride invites judgment.

verses.text: Go to Calneh, and see. From there go to Hamath the great. Then go down to Gath of the Philistines. Are they better than these kingdoms? Is their border greater than your border?
verses.arminianNotes: Israel is told to look at Calneh, Hamath, and Gath. Interpreters debate whether the point is that Israel is no better than these kingdoms, or that their fate is a warning. Arminian readers leave the dating of these cities’ falls open and keep the warning in view.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hold the historical details loosely and hear the comparison as deflating national pride. Shared ground: Israel’s size and success are no protection, and the nations around them show that kingdoms rise and fall under God’s hand.

verses.text: Alas for you who put far away the evil day, and cause the seat of violence to come near,
verses.arminianNotes: They “put far away the evil day” while they “cause the seat of violence to come near”. Arminian readers see self-deception: denying judgment while hastening it through injustice, a choice with real consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same irony and stress that sin blinds people to danger. Shared ground: refusing to think about the day of reckoning does not delay it; violence in the land brings it near.

verses.text: who lie on beds of ivory, and stretch themselves on their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the middle of the stall,
verses.arminianNotes: They “lie on beds of ivory” and eat choice lambs and calves. Arminian readers note that wealth itself is not condemned, but luxury enjoyed without compassion, while the poor suffer under the same leaders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the same contrast and stress that self-indulgence reveals where the heart rests. Shared ground: the picture of lounging and feasting shows a people at ease who have forgotten both God and neighbor.

verses.text: who strum on the strings of a harp, who invent for themselves instruments of music, like David;
verses.arminianNotes: They “invent for themselves instruments of music, like David”. The comparison with David is debated: it may mock their pretensions, or note skill used only for pleasure. Arminian readers keep the main point: gifts enjoyed with no thought for God’s purposes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also leave the precise sense open while noting that David’s music served worship. Shared ground: the leaders take the forms of a godly heritage and turn them toward their own amusement.

verses.text: who drink wine in bowls, and anoint themselves with the best oils, but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph.
verses.arminianNotes: They drink from bowls and use the best oils, “but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph.” Arminian readers see indifference as the central sin, a refusal to share in the suffering of the people they should protect.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same lack of grief as evidence of hearts untouched by God’s concern for his people. Shared ground: comfort is not condemned for its own sake, but comfort that is blind to the ruin of others is judged.

verses.text: Therefore they will now go captive with the first who go captive. The feasting and lounging will end.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore they will now go captive with the first who go captive.” Arminian readers see poetic justice: those first in privilege will be first into exile, and “The feasting and lounging will end.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same reversal as God’s just sentence on the proud. Shared ground: those who led the nation in luxury will lead it into captivity, and the end of their feasting is certain.

verses.text: “The Lord GOD has sworn by himself,” says the LORD, the God of Armies: “I abhor the pride of Jacob, and detest his fortresses. Therefore I will deliver up the city with all that is in it.
verses.arminianNotes: “The Lord GOD has sworn by himself,” says the LORD: “I abhor the pride of Jacob”. Arminian readers see pride as the root of the people’s self-reliance, and God’s oath by himself shows that his own character guarantees the judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that God swears by himself because there is none greater, binding his word to his nature. Shared ground: God detests the pride that trusts in fortresses, and he will deliver up the city with all that is in it.

verses.text: It will happen that if ten men remain in one house, they will die.
verses.arminianNotes: The warning that “if ten men remain in one house, they will die” reaches even the survivors. Arminian readers see the severity of judgment here; the picture suggests plague following war, though the text does not specify.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same thoroughness of the judgment and note that the number ten echoes the shrinking counts of 5:3. Shared ground: no house can hide from the judgment God has sworn.

verses.text: “When a man’s relative carries him, even he who burns him, to bring bodies out of the house, and asks him who is in the innermost parts of the house, ‘Is there yet any with you?’ And he says, ‘No;’ then he will say, ‘Hush! Indeed we must not mention the LORD’s name.’
verses.arminianNotes: A relative comes to carry out bodies, and the one who burns him may refer to burning bodies or burning spices for the dead; interpreters differ. A survivor answers “No” and is hushed: “Indeed we must not mention the LORD’s name.” Arminian readers hear dread of drawing more judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hold the burial detail loosely and see the hush as fear of the LORD whose name had been taken lightly. Shared ground: a people who presumed on God’s name now fear even to speak it, a grim reversal of their earlier ease.

verses.text: “For, behold, the LORD commands, and the great house will be smashed to pieces, and the little house into bits.
verses.arminianNotes: “For, behold, the LORD commands, and the great house will be smashed to pieces, and the little house into bits.” Arminian readers note that judgment falls on great and small alike, so no one escapes because of rank.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s command as the decisive cause of the destruction. Shared ground: the LORD’s word is effective, and both mansions and small homes are shattered when he commands.

verses.text: Do horses run on the rocky crags? Does one plow there with oxen? But you have turned justice into poison, and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness,
verses.arminianNotes: “Do horses run on the rocky crags? Does one plow there with oxen?” Arminian readers see the absurd questions exposing how unnatural it is to turn “justice into poison,” a choice against the grain of creation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same proverbial logic showing the perversity of sin. Shared ground: just as no one plows rocks with oxen, no one should turn justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness.

verses.text: you who rejoice in a thing of nothing, who say, ‘Haven’t we taken for ourselves horns by our own strength?’
verses.arminianNotes: They “rejoice in a thing of nothing” and boast of taking “horns by our own strength”. Many interpreters hear wordplay on town names (often identified as Lo-debar and Karnaim), though the text as translated does not name them. Arminian readers stress the folly of self-made confidence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the possible wordplay and stress that boasting in human strength robs God of glory. Shared ground: victories credited to “our own strength” are a thing of nothing compared with the LORD who gives and takes away.

verses.text: For, behold, I will raise up against you a nation, house of Israel,” says the LORD, the God of Armies; “and they will afflict you from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of the Arabah.”
verses.arminianNotes: “I will raise up against you a nation,” says the LORD, the God of Armies. The text does not name the nation. Arminian readers see God using the nations to judge his people, while the invading nation remains responsible for its own actions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God sovereignly raising up the instrument of judgment. The phrase “from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of the Arabah” covers the land Israel had gained. Shared ground: the God who gave Israel its borders can bring affliction across them.
